title: Supreme Court temporarily allowed immigration stops challenged as discriminatory
description_medium: On September 8, 2025, the Supreme Court granted the federal government's request to stay a district court order limiting immigration stops in the Los Angeles area while the government's appeal proceeded. The order temporarily lifted that restriction; it did not finally decide the case or give ICE general permission to stop people solely because of skin color. The title's description of the ruling as approval of racial profiling overstates the interim order.
description_long: The Supreme Court's September 8, 2025 order in Noem v. Vasquez Perdomo granted the federal government's application to stay a district court order while the government pursued an appeal. The lower-court order had restricted immigration stops in the Los Angeles area amid allegations that agents relied on factors including race, language, location and type of work. By granting the stay, the Court temporarily removed that particular restriction during the appeal; it did not issue a final decision on the underlying claims or a general ruling that skin color alone is a lawful basis for a stop. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote separately, discussing circumstances in which an officer might consider several factors together. The supplied event title collapses an interim procedural order into a broad endorsement of racial profiling. The official order supports a more limited account focused on the temporary stay and ongoing litigation. It does not establish how officers conducted later stops or decide the plaintiffs' ultimate constitutional claims. The docket and eventual appellate disposition are needed to describe the case's final outcome.
evidence_notes: The Supreme Court's order dated September 8 grants a stay pending appeal; this is interim relief, not final merits resolution. It stayed the July 11 district court order.
corrected_wording: The Supreme Court temporarily stayed a lower-court restriction on immigration stops in Los Angeles pending appeal; do not say it broadly approved skin-color-only profiling.
exact_blocker: The packet headline misstates the scope and posture of the Court's interim order; final appellate disposition is not supplied.

The policy barred journalists from seeking or using certain information that the Defense Department had not authorized for release, including material that was not classified. News organizations faced a choice between signing the rules and retaining their Pentagon credentials or refusing and giving up their badges. The linked account reports that major outlets rejected the requirements; contemporary reporting described broad refusals across newspapers, broadcasters and wire services. Those responses turned the policy into a dispute over press access and the ability to report on the military.
